title: Internal Spearphishing
summary: Internal Spearphishing is targeted phishing sent from a trusted account inside the victim organisation instead of from an outside address. The pattern is multi stage: the attacker first controls either a device or the credentials of a real user, then uses that mailbox, calendar or chat identity to reach colleagues, partners or privileged staff. Because the message arrives from a known sender, inside the mail flow, it passes sender authentication checks that would normally reject an external lure, and it often carries an impersonation touch such as a display name that matches a manager or a finance team. Delivery mechanisms are the familiar ones, including malicious attachments and links that lead to a credential harvesting page or a payload, and internal chat platforms are used to move files or persuade staff to hand over information. The artefacts are internal: messages between two internal mailboxes with unusual attachments or external links, mailbox rules and delegated access created just before sending, new sign in locations for the sending account, and chat messages from an identity that behaves differently from its normal history. Distinguishing it from ordinary internal mail depends on catching the anomaly in the sending account rather than the reputation of the sender domain.

beginner.definition: This technique is a phishing message sent from inside your own company. The sender account is real, but an attacker is using it. The message looks like normal mail from a colleague.
beginner.whyItMatters: People trust mail from their own colleagues, so they click more often. Filters that block unknown outside senders cannot help here. One stolen account can be used to reach many more people. Chat apps spread the same trick very quickly.
howItWorks: The attacker first takes over one account by stealing its password or by controlling the device that uses it.
They study the mailbox for a short time. They look for who sends money, who approves things and who holds rights.
They then send mail from that real account, often pretending to be a manager or a finance colleague.
The message may carry an attached file or a link. Both are ways to install software or capture a password.
Links usually open a fake login page. This is a copy of a real page that records whatever you type.
Chat apps such as team messaging tools are used in the same way, because staff trust a message from a known name.
beginner.example: Think of a school office. A stranger copies the head teacher's voice and calls the reception desk from inside the building. The receptionist hears a familiar voice and a familiar request, so the cash box is opened. Nothing about the call came from outside, and the phone log simply shows an internal extension.
takeaways: Trust comes from the account, not the person, so a message from a colleague can still be an attack.
Verify unusual money or password requests through a second channel such as a phone call you start yourself.
Watch for account changes like new mail rules and logins from strange places, because those often come first.

objectives: Define internal spearphishing and explain how it differs from phishing that starts outside the organisation.
Describe how a compromised account or device is used as the launching point for later messages.
Identify the mailbox and chat artefacts that suggest an internal account has been hijacked.
Explain why sender authentication checks do not stop messages sent from a genuine internal account.
Describe the verification habits that reduce the chance of a colleague being tricked by an internal lure.
